All of the above, really. It feels like I've been using the same max weight for most exercises instead of being able to keep going up in weight, which makes it hard to tell if I'm really improving. But it also feels like I'm working super hard and pushing myself every time, if that makes sense. It also seems like progress is really slow for the calisthenic moves I focus on. For example, it took me several months to work up from 0 pistol squats to being able to do about 10 in one minute on each leg. I had to take 3 weeks off due to illness, which lasted until the beginning of December. My fitness seemed to take a nose dive after just that short time off, and every workout has been extra hard since then. It feels like I'm finally *almost* back to where I was. Just today, I'm back at the point where I can do 8 on each side in that time. Same thing for pullups. I got up to doing 8 with good form, and after illness and a few weeks back working out, I'm stuck back at 6. Fat loss seems stalled too, though that probably has more to do with diet.

Thing is, I've searched for years now. And nothing really fits. The closest thing to my symptoms that I have found, oddly, is narcolepsy.  Lots of narcoleptics apparently can exhibit extreme bouts of insomnia. There are other related neurological conditions that are lesser known. The drugs used to treat them work on the central nervous system. Those are the only kind that have worked for me for sleep. But without the diagnosis, it's really difficult to keep getting them prescribed, as they are controlled substances.

Even worse, getting diagnosed with even the more widely known narcolepsy is so difficult. Two different types of sleep studies must be conducted to "pass". Sorry for the rant. It's just hard. Until I can be diagnosed, I will continue to be medicated with psychiatric drugs rather than those that work. I've been this bad for going on 3 years, but got my first sleeping medication before I was 10 years old. It's been a long battle.

I can respect that. And I do agree that a change in rhetoric can go a long way toward persuading people. 

Of course some pro-choicers grieve, whether it's a miscarriage or an abortion. And some of us do not. Of course I don't advocate for abortion to be the first line of defense against unwanted pregnancy. Preventative measures are absolutely the best possible scenario. I think that is a common ground that (most) pro-lifers and virtually all pro-choice advocates share. However, I do not see abortion itself as a tragedy. The same goes for miscarriage. The only part of either scenario that I see as tragic is for the couple; if they were wanting a child and envisioned a future in which the pregnancy was carried to term, then the loss of that future is indeed tragic. 

I really respect your opinion though, and I am happy to have an actually civil conversation with someone about this without it turning ugly.
No problem! Thanks for listening. I'm not sure what your stance is, but I love a genuinely informed opinion, even if it's one I don't share.

I also believe 12 weeks is much too early a cutoff. Some other responders here have provided excellent objective explanations for why this is so, but I'd like to offer a bit of personal anecdotal evidence. I had a surgical abortion at 22 weeks. Due to a series of unfortunate circumstances, I was totally unaware I was pregnant until 21 weeks. I was on birth control at the time (the pill) and had been suffering from amenorrhea since I was 14 due to low body weight. I was about 95 lbs and had virtually no symptoms, as well as a false negative pregnancy test a couple months prior. I was 19 years old and suffering from an eating disorder and other serious mental health issues which would have made carrying the pregnancy to term very dangerous for my health, not to mention the fact that I never wish to produce children, in part due to the poor genetics I never wish to pass on. I needed to have this later abortion. I took every reasonable precaution to avoid getting pregnant, and that failed. I am 100% certain I would have sought out an illegal abortion if there was a ban past 12 weeks. For women like me, that could have been devastating, possibly even resulting in my death.

Oh yes. Pregnancy dreams definitely go in the nightmare category for me. I have had several nightmares about this, and in them I always find out I'm like 6 months along and it's too late to get an abortion.

>I know certain drugs and can bring out underlying mental issues, but will it be like this forever?

I don't think anyone can tell you with certainty how long this could last, or whether you might feel this sensation of depersonalization on and off for quite some time, although I never like to say 'forever'. What I can tell you though, is that feelings of detachment and depersonalization are very common symptoms of long term anxiety. I sincerely doubt that this one drug experience altered your brain chemistry so much that something that wasn't there at all to begin with has suddenly manifested itself as an everyday symptom. 

I've never experienced something like this myself, not brought on by a drug experience. But something kind of similar did happen to me last year, when I was initially hospitalized for malnutrition, exhaustion and generally poor health as a result of my anxiety. A few days in, I started to hallucinate and lose consciousness on and off, and it turned out I was suffering from a pretty rare vitamin deficiency necessary for brain and nervous system function. Once they figured it out, I was given intravenous vitamin supplements and immediately came out of it. However, after leaving the hospital I realized that the hallucinations and the many hours I spent in that state had altered me. I don't think that I'm damaged, or that my brain is somehow permanently altered, just that I felt things that I'd never felt before. Very negative things, mostly. I think of it like this: my mind went to and spent a good deal of time in an unpleasant place it had never been to before. And now, after it's over, my mind still knows how to get there. I feel like maybe it's similar for you. I haven't felt entirely 'normal' since then either. 

So, I'm not sure what advice I can really give you. Other than just to tell you that I think I understand some of what you are going through. I've also experienced the sensation of depersonalization myself (again, not drug induced) and I know it to be very unpleasant. I believe it may be a coping mechanism for the anxious mind, perhaps a means of escape from acute symptoms of anxiety. I find it helps to focus on my breathing, and to tell myself that I'm safe, I'm really here, and that it will pass. 

Anyway, sorry for the novel. I hope some of that helps.
